hops.title: Black widow venom empties a nerve terminal
hops.text: Del Castillo and Katz turned transmitter release down to a trickle so they could see single packets. Black widow spider venom sends spontaneous release soaring. Applied to a frog nerve-muscle junction in a calcium-free bath, it drove miniature endplate potentials to about 1,500 per second. Within thirty minutes the terminal had released roughly 700,000 packets and then fell nearly silent, emptied of quanta and of synaptic vesicles. With calcium in the bath, release rose to similar peaks and stayed near 400 packets per second for up to an hour, totaling at least 1.5 million packets in that period, more than twice the estimated upper limit for the resting store.

sources.citation: Fesce R, Segal JR, Ceccarelli B, Hurlbut WP. Effects of black widow spider venom and Ca2+ on quantal secretion at the frog neuromuscular junction. J Gen Physiol. 1986;88(1):59–81 (PMID 3488369).

image.caption: In a calcium-free bath, a venom-treated frog nerve terminal released an estimated 700,000 packets in half an hour.

hops.title: Botox does not kill the nerve
hops.text: It is easy to assume Botox smooths a frown by numbing or killing the nerve. It does neither. Botulinum toxin type A acts inside the motor nerve terminal and cuts SNAP-25, one of the SNARE proteins that zip a vesicle to the membrane. Docked vesicles now rarely manage to fuse, so far fewer packets of acetylcholine are released and the muscle relaxes. The effect wears off: in the original frown-line trials it lasted a median of about 120 days. Jean Carruthers, the Vancouver physician who helped start the cosmetic use in 1987, used it on herself as well, partly to reassure patients worried about having a poison injected.

sources.citation: Schiavo G, Rossetto O, Catsicas S, et al. Identification of the nerve terminal targets of botulinum neurotoxin serotypes A, D, and E. J Biol Chem. 1993;268(32):23784–23787 (PMID 8226912).
Scott AB. Botulinum toxin injection into extraocular muscles as an alternative to strabismus surgery. Ophthalmology. 1980;87(10):1044–1049 (PMID 7243198).

Carruthers J, Carruthers A, Blitzer A, Eadie N, Brin MF. Treatment of glabellar lines with Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA): Development, insights, and impact. Medicine (Baltimore). 2023;102(S1):e32375 (PMC10374180).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A relaxed man in a bathrobe smiling at his smooth forehead in a round bathroom mirror.
image.caption: Botox cuts SNAP-25, reducing acetylcholine release and weakening the muscle until the effect wears off.

hops.afterHeading: Count or size? When the safety factor fails
hops.title: Mary Walker and the curare clue
hops.text: In 1927, a leading medical textbook offered people with myasthenia gravis bed rest, careful feeding and tonics. In 1934, Mary Walker, a Scottish physician practicing outside academic medicine, built on the observation that the weakness resembled poisoning by the arrow poison curare and reasoned that physostigmine, a drug that counters curare, might help. She gave it to a 56-year-old woman, whose strength returned rapidly and dramatically, though only for a while. Her trial helped establish anticholinesterases for myasthenia gravis decades before anyone showed antibodies attacking acetylcholine receptors. By slowing acetylcholinesterase, the drug lets each packet do more, so the weakened endplate potential can reach threshold for a muscle impulse again.

sources.citation: Manu P, Rogozea LM, Roman-Filip C. Pharmacological Management of Myasthenia Gravis: A Century of Expert Opinions in Cecil Textbook of Medicine. Am J Ther. 2021;28(6):e631–e637 (PMID 34757964).

Farmakidis C, Pasnoor M, Dimachkie MM, Barohn RJ. Treatment of Myasthenia Gravis. Neurol Clin. 2018;36(2):311–337 (PMC6690491); McCarter SJ et al., J R Coll Physicians Edinb. 2019;49(3):255–259 (PMID 31497797).
